s06.slug: SUNDAY · 5:25 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE PORCH — THE PHONE THAT RINGS AT THE KICKOFF
body: The anthem comes through the screen door with the volume up full, Carrie Underwood alone at a microphone over seventy thousand people in Miami, and the front room gets to its feet for it. Celeste stands at her corner of the couch with a hand on Remy’s shoulder. Mémère comes up out of her armchair on Kevin’s arm and stands with the beads hanging from the hand she holds over her heart. Clovis has his visor off and pressed to his chest. The twins have come out from under the table. At the far end of the couch Laney has her chin up and is mouthing every word, and Margot stands because everybody else is standing, hands in her back pockets, watching them do it. Lena stands on the rug beside him in her socks with her hands clasped behind her back. Lucille sleeps through it on her mother’s shoulder in the black-and-gold cap.

It ends, and the house yells, and the yell comes back down Dupre Street out of every open door on the block, a hair ahead or a hair behind, depending on whose set it is. The coin goes up in Miami. The room takes the coin personally.

When the teams go out to line up, Jack gets up off the rug with the RAZR in his hand. She asked him for a call at the kickoff. The screen door bangs behind him on its spring, and through the screen he sees Lena’s eyes come off Miami to the door.

Out here it’s nearly dark. The sun has gone down behind the houses across the street and taken most of the color with it, and the porch light isn’t on yet, so the light comes from the windows: every house on Dupre Street with its door open and its television going, the same blue flicker on a row of porch ceilings down to the corner. The street itself is empty. Cars parked solid on both sides, fleur-de-lis on the bumpers, and not a soul on the sidewalk, not a bicycle, not a dog. A city has gone indoors at once and is holding still in there.

Ferd’s folding chair stands empty by the rail with an Abita sweating on the boards beside it; he went in for the anthem and hasn’t come back. Tony hasn’t moved. He sits in the kitchen chair with his back to the window and his elbows on his knees, and the transistor stands on the rail at his elbow with its face turned toward him and the coat-hanger antenna pointed east, at Miami, in case that helps. The WWL men are on it, fast and low and already hoarse. Tony’s eyes are shut. His lips are going. He doesn’t look round when the door bangs, or when Jack sits down on the top step a yard from his shoe.
Jack opens the RAZR to call her, and it rings in his hand, open, with his thumb still on its way to the keys: SKYE (MISFIT), across the inside screen. She got there first. He presses the green key.
“Don’t say hello,” Skye says. “Is it on? Tell me it isn’t on yet.”
“They’re lining up.”

“Good. I made it.” On her end something hums, a space heater or a generator, and under the hum, small and tinny, a television that isn’t his: the same game, the same men in the same booth, half a second behind the radio at Tony’s elbow. “I’m in the trailer. It’s three-thirty here. It’s *Sunday*. Nobody on this crew knows it’s Sunday. I told the makeup lady at lunch, and she said, ‘Is it?’ and went back to her crossword.”
“What are you watching it on?”

“Kyle’s laptop. Kyle is a PA. Kyle is from Fort Wayne, Indiana, and he is the only person in this province who cares, and he cares for the wrong team, and he has lent me his laptop and his hat. I’m in a Colts cap, Jack.”
“You said into a wig.”

“I’m wearing it into the wig. Cassie’s wig. It’s a long story.” A chair creaks under her, a chair that has been sat back in before. “It’s auburn, it took an hour, and it’s held onto my actual head with about forty pins, so it can’t come off between setups, so the cap goes on top. I look like a Colts fan who’s been through something.”
“You said quietly.”

“I am cheering quietly. Kyle and I have a chant. It’s very quiet. It’s mostly eyebrows.” The heater hums. “There are three other people in here and none of them care. The makeup lady has her crossword. A driver named Gord is asleep sitting up with a bran muffin in his hand. And Cassie’s stand-in, who is wearing the wig’s little sister, asked me which ones are the Saints, and I said the ones in the gold pants, and she said, ‘Oh, nice,’ like it was something they’d decided this morning.”
Jack laughs, and keeps it down for the porch.
“Where are you?” Skye says. “Don’t say a porch.”
“A porch.”
“Who’s on it?”
“Mr. Broussard.”
“Do him,” she says. “Three sentences.”
Tony is a yard from his shoulder with his eyes shut. Jack bends his head down toward the steps and keeps his voice under the radio.

“He sells fish on Banks Street, and in 1980 he wore a bag over his head at the Dome, and he’s been sending God the bill for it ever since. He couldn’t watch the Vikings, so he’s out here with his eyes shut and a radio with a coat hanger in it. His lips are going, and it isn’t the rosary.”
“Oh, I love him,” Skye says. “Tell him I’m sorry about the Colts in advance. Tell him I’m *personally* sorry.”
Jack looks at Tony. Tony’s lips go on moving.
“He’s on the other line.”
“Then I’ll hold.” Paper moves on her end, a page, a cover. “I have news. I bought it.”
“Bought what?”

“*The Moviegoer*. At the airport in San Francisco on Friday, at the newsstand, between a book about abs and a book about a vampire. Because of the margins. I read it on the plane, and the plane wasn’t long enough, so I finished it in the back of the car with the fleece man, and he asked me if it was any good, and I said I didn’t know yet. It hadn’t been read to me.”
“And?”

“And I have a note. For Binx.” A page turns on her end, and turns back. “Binx goes to the movies so his street will be real. I’ve *been* the movie since I was eleven. Being in it doesn’t make anything real either. You know what does? A man reading you something rude at a gas pump.”

Down the block a screen door opens and a man yells into the street for somebody named Darnell to get in here, it’s starting, and the door slaps shut again. Jack sits with the phone against his ear and his other hand over his mouth.
“Yeah,” he says.

“Okay,” Skye says. “Enough literature.” And then the voice comes down, close to the phone, low, the one she keeps for him, in a trailer in Canada with a crossword going on three feet away. “Wardrobe let me have your shirt back for lunch. Ten minutes. Cassie’s very possessive; it had to be negotiated.” The chair creaks. “I’m not telling you what else I had on.”
Jack looks for some time at a Buick parked across the street.
Tony’s eyes stay shut.
“I owe you a picture,” Skye says.
“Do you.”
“Not today. The wardrobe lady sits right outside that door, and she has opinions about my elbows.” And then, in the same breath, the same size: “Did you go up this morning?”
“I went up.”

“Good.” She says it short, and then she yawns, enormously, into the phone, and doesn’t apologize for it. “I’m so tired, Jack. I’ve been Cassie since six. Cassie cried in the rain at eleven and again at two, and the rain is a man named Russ on a ladder with a hose, and I have to go cry in front of Russ again in about five minutes.” The little television behind her goes to a commercial, a Canadian bank, a man in a canoe. “Hang on.”
A click, and the television in Burnaby is gone. There’s only the heater, and her breathing, close.
“There,” she says. “I turned Canada off. I wanted to hear the kickoff where you are.”
Jack takes the phone down from his ear and holds it out in the air between the radio and the screen door, and Tony doesn’t open his eyes.

In Miami the ball goes up. It comes over the transistor and through the screen door at the same time, the WWL man’s voice climbing with it and the house going up underneath, a yell and a groan and Mémère saying something sharp in French and Remy saying something worse in English, and a half-second after that Dupre Street does it again out of every open door on the block, and down at the corner somebody leans on a car horn in the rhythm of the Who Dat. Tony’s hands close into fists.
Jack puts the phone back to his ear. Skye is laughing.

“Oh, I *heard* that,” she says. “I heard the *street*.” Two knuckles knock on a door on her end, and a man’s voice through it says they’re ready for her in the rain. “That’s Russ,” Skye says. “That’s my hose.”

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Monday she picked Danny’s birthday book on State Street — O’Connor, all the stories — and wrote the card herself, in capitals. She says Gretta’s the only one at that party who isn’t acting. At a red light the radio played it, the day before his birthday, and we sang it at each other with the top down. Somebody filmed it. Tuesday her people were on the phone by six. She didn’t share it; she wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about her job. She kissed me on the Morro steps in front of everybody and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Then Danny called on his birthday and she got on the phone. She told him I tricked her. Then she told him the truth: she was about to leave when I walked over, and she still has the book, with CON crossed out. Candlemas she held my candle while I knelt. That night she came up to my room for the first time. She didn’t ask. When she asks again, she says, she wants me to have nowhere to be in the morning. She asked if there’s a version of later she’s in. Wednesday on the swing, coats on, she kept me in the daylight. She’s in Vancouver for two weeks, a pilot, from Friday. She told me to go to New Orleans and watch my Saints win. Maybe it’ll be good for you guys, she said. I said yes. Thursday we skipped the rest of the day for the Point. Sol let her into the darkroom in January, for the project. Thursday night it was full of me — asleep, the back of me on the Point, the two of us on the swing — pictures I didn’t know anybody was taking. She gave me the swing: NOT FOR POSTING. It’s in Hale’s book. She propped the door open on purpose. She asked. She was the one who said no. Her father called her Mary Kate. He left in the dark for a five o’clock call when she was four, kissed her, told her to go back to sleep, and didn’t come back. Everybody she’s ever loved had a call time. When I come back she wants the truth, to her face. I promised. She drove me up the hill at three and waited in the Saab under the bell tower with three suitcases in the back. Friday at a quarter to five she stood with us in the lot while Osei blessed the van, with her eyes shut, and looked at the water on the back of her hand. Bye, Coat check. She went north. We went south. Friday at a truck stop under Picacho Peak she called from Burnaby. Wardrobe took my flannel: Cassie wears it; it got the part. The geese are the size of Labradors. I read her one of Hale’s rude ones at the pump. Saturday night she called again after wrap, and I read her two more, on the Broussards’ front steps. I told Lena’s little sister who she is. My girlfriend. In Canada. She wants a call at the kickoff. Sunday at the kickoff I had the phone open to call her, and it rang in my hand. She was in a trailer in Burnaby in a Colts cap, wearing it into Cassie’s wig. She bought her own *Moviegoer* at the airport and read it on the plane. Being in the movie doesn’t make anything real either, she says. She owes me a picture. Not today.

choices.text: “Love you. Go cheer for the wrong people.”
choices.key: At the kickoff Skye called first, from a trailer in Burnaby, in a Colts cap. On Tony’s porch you told her you love her.
response: “Love you,” he says. “Go cheer for the wrong people.”
He doesn’t bring it down for the porch. It goes out over the rail into Dupre Street at the size he says everything else, with Tony a yard away.
“Love you,” Skye says. “Go be loud.” The knuckles again, and Russ. “Bye, Who Dat.”

The RAZR shuts on its cracked hinge. Tony’s eyes stay shut. He reaches out to the rail and takes the transistor by its two top corners and turns it a little further toward himself, until its face is square on his, and sets his elbows back on his knees.
Jack gets up off the step. As the screen door opens under his hand, behind him Tony says to the radio, “*Huh.*”
The WWL men go on talking to him about field position.

choices.text: “Tell the wig the Colts are favored by five.”
choices.key: At the kickoff Skye called first, from a trailer in Burnaby, in a Colts cap. You told her to tell the wig the Colts are favored by five.
response: “Tell the wig the Colts are favored by five.”
“The wig knows,” Skye says. “The wig has money on it. Kyle set the line.” The knuckles again, harder; Russ is not a patient hose. “Bye, Who Dat.”

He folds the phone shut. Tony hasn’t moved; his lips haven’t stopped. Jack gets up off the top step and pulls the screen door open, and the spring stretches and sings and brings the door round after him, and it catches him on the heel on his way in.

choices.text: “You’d like this porch. You’d have him doing his voice in ten minutes.”
choices.key: At the kickoff Skye called first, from a trailer in Burnaby, in a Colts cap. You told her she’d like this porch. Five minutes, she said.
response: “You’d like this porch,” he says. “You’d have him doing his voice in ten minutes.”
“Five,” Skye says. “I’d have the bag story by the second quarter, and I’d have the bag.” Russ knocks again. She doesn’t hurry for him. “Bye, Who Dat.”
The hinge creaks shut. He sits a moment longer on the step with it in his hand, and Tony goes on with God, and Jack gets up and lets himself into the noise.
On the rug Lena’s head turns as he comes in. She moves her bowl off his half of the rug and turns back to the game.

s06a.slug: SUNDAY · 5:50 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE FRONT ROOM — THE FIRST QUARTER
body: The window behind Mémère’s lamp has gone dark blue, and the only other light in the front room comes off Miami.

The Saints get the ball first and give it back. The Colts take it down the field in a straight line, Manning at the line with his hands going, pointing at things and changing them, and when it stalls Stover kicks it through from thirty-eight and it’s three to nothing. The Saints get the ball and give it back again. The Colts go the length of the field a second time, slower and worse, and Manning finds Garçon in the end zone, and it is ten to nothing, and the front room of a raised shotgun on Dupre Street takes it every way a room can.

Clovis gets up out of his folding chair by the door and sings the first verse of “When the Saints” straight at the television, a cappella, loud enough to rattle the screen, and at the end of the first verse he stops, as advertised, and sits back down, and the second verse goes unsung. Mémère’s beads go faster. Kevin, on the dining chair at her elbow, keeps up with her a decade behind and losing ground. Remy has slid down the arm of the couch until he is mostly on Celeste, with his Saints cap over his face.
“It’s early,” Celeste whispers, to Remy, to the room, to the cap.
“Mama says it’s *early*,” Josie relays from under the dining table, and Jude, beside her, eats a Zapp’s.

On the floor by the television Tess has Lucille up on her shoulder, and Lucille is asleep through all of it with her fists up by her ears, like a very small fighter between rounds. Aints III gets up off Jack’s feet, turns around twice, and lies back down facing away from the screen.
“This is structure,” Theo announces from the far end of the couch. “Every great sports picture is down ten in the first act. You don’t make a movie about the team that’s up ten.”
“Theo,” Laney says, with her fingers sunk in a stuffed football from Carrollton, “I will put you on that porch.”
Margot, on the footstool, with her knees up under her chin: “Fascinating. The room has gone directly from denial to bargaining. It skipped anger.”
“It did not skip anger,” says Remy, under the cap.
The camera finds number 93 on the Colts’ sideline, bouncing on his toes between series, and Lena, beside Jack on the rug, says through her teeth, “Look at him. Indianapolis lies about ankles.”

At the break the room breathes out and half of it goes for the kitchen. Remy lifts the cap. On the big screen the cars and the beer give way to something quieter: a woman with her hair done nicely, talking soft into the camera about the son she nearly lost, and the son, when he comes, is Tim Tebow, coming in from the side of the frame to take his mother down in a tackle, which is the joke, and then a web address, and then it’s a car again. Thirty seconds.
“*Gator*,” Remy says, with feeling, and puts the cap back over his face.

Margot has not moved. “I’d like to be very precise about this,” she says. “For years CBS hasn’t taken advocacy in the Super Bowl. They turned down MoveOn in 2004. This year they took that one. And this same week they turned down an ad for a dating site, because it was two men on a couch, kissing.” She lets her chin come off her knees. “So the policy is: advocacy is fine if it’s *your* advocacy.”
She looks at Kevin. Kevin is looking at the television. His hands are on his knees.
“It’s a mother saying she’s glad she had her kid,” Jack says. “If that’s too controversial for television, television’s got a problem.”

“It’s a mother saying it in thirty seconds bought by an organization with a legislative agenda,” Margot says, “on the network that just told two men their couch wasn’t fit for Sunday. Which is advocacy, Jack, which you know, and which you’re delighted about.”
“I am delighted about it.”
“I know. It’s unbearable.”

Lena has been eating Zapp’s out of the bag in her lap one at a time, and she points the next one at the screen, where the car is now going up a mountain. “Y’all are both wrong. Two and a half million dollars. Do you know how many diapers two and a half million dollars is? In this city? For girls who don’t have a Heisman coming?”
“That’s not the —”

“It is *exactly* the.” She eats the chip. “And it wasn’t brave. It was careful. Thirty seconds and not one word in it a network lawyer could get a splinter off. It’s a holy card. It’s a very nice holy card. You could hand it out at a wake.”
“Careful’s how you get it on CBS.”
“Careful’s how you get it on CBS and nowhere else.”
Her knee is against his on the rug through all of it, and takes no part in the argument.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, from the dining chair, “it’s the first quarter.”
Through the screen door, from the porch, at the volume of a man who sells fish for a living: “*Y’ALL HUSH.*”
The room hushes. In the quiet the transistor on the rail can be heard going on outside about third down, and Mémère’s beads, and the refrigerator.
At the far end of the couch Laney has the stuffed football turned over in her hands. She is still looking at the screen where the mother was, though it’s a truck now.
“It was just his mama,” she says.
